Final Exam

Naomi Liftman

December 3, 2025

Problem 1

Fit appropriate regression models for fatigue (SSC-F) given weakness (SSC-W) and treatment group (IC). Select the regression model that is best supported by the data using the likelihood ratio test, AIC and BIC. Please justify your answers in writing and with code.

We will start by fitting a model with only fatigue in the model. We can then fit a model of fatigue given weakness and a model of fatigue given treatment group. We can then fit two models for fatigue given weakness and treatment, one where it is weakness plus treatment and one where it is the interaction of weakness and treatment. So in total we can fit five models. For each of these models we will then find the AIC and BIC scores. All of this can be found below in table 1.

What we can see from table 1 is that based on AIC and BIC scores model four fits our data the best (we are looking for the smallest AIC and BIC scores). However, we can see that both model two and five have similar BIC and AIC scores. Thus we may want to use a likelihood ratio test to compare each of these models to model four. When we compare model two to model four we see that we have a p-value of 0.03415. What this means is that model four is significantly more accurate than model two at the \(\alpha = .05\) level. We can perform the same tests for model five versus model four which returns a p-value of 0.3425. This means that we do not have evidence to suggest that model model four is significantly more accurate than model five. So we believe they are relatively similar in accuracy; however, since the non-interaction model (model 4) is less complicated we are inclined to use this model.

We have used AIC, BIC, and likelihood ratio tests to show that Model 4 is the best model we can fit to represent our data. This model is \(Fatigue = Weakness + Treatement Group\).

Problem 2

Fit appropriate regression models for weakness (SSC-W) given fatigue (SSC-F) and treatment group (IC). Select the regression model that is best supported by the data using the likelihood ratio test, AIC and BIC. Please justify your answers in writing and with code.

We will follow very similarly the steps we followed in problem 1. Our first model will be only weakness, then weakness given fatigue, weakness given treatment group, and then the two models with both fatigue and treatment group. To see each model and their AIC and BIC scores see table 2 below.

We can see that once again our best model based on AIC and BIC scores is the fourth model. We can also see that model 2 and five have similar AIC and BIC scores. Thus we will again return to the likelihood ratio tests. When we test model 2 against model 4 we get a p-value of 0.006746. This is smaller than our \(\alpha = .05\) so we will reject the null hypothesis that these models fit the data equally well and we will find that model 4 is significantly more accurate. When we perform the ratio test between model 4 and 5 we find that our p-value is 0.3425. This is larger than our p-value and so we will fail to reject the null hypothesis. Thus we do not have evidence to suggest that model 4 is more accurate than model 5. However, since model four is less complicated than model 5 and has a better AIC and BIC we will use that model.

We have used AIC, BIC, and likelihood ratio tests to show that Model 4 is the best model we can fit to represent our data. This model is \(Weakness = Fatigue + Treatement Group\).

Problem 3

Fit loglinear models for weakness (SSC-W), fatigue (SSC-F) and treatment group (IC). Select the loglinear model that is best supported by the data using \(G^2\). Please justify your answers in writing and with code.

In total we will look at eight models. The first is the fully saturated log-linear regression model. We fit this saturated model and then perform a chi-squared test based on \(G^2\). What we find here is that the p-value is zero, which means that we reject the null hypothesis and conclude this model does not fit our data well. We can then look at the three models (labeled models 2-4) which are a single variable independent of the other two variables. Again we find no p-values above our \(\alpha = 0.01\) threshold and conclude that these models do not fit our data well. We then fit the three models with conditionals on a variable and find that two of these three models (labeled 5-7) have a chi-squared p-value of above 0.01. Thus we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that models 5 and 6 fit our data well. We can then fit the final model which is our model stating there are no three factor interactions. This model also has a p-value of above 0.01 and thus we again fail to reject the null hypothesis and find this model fits the data well. All of this can be seen below in table 3.

While we are thankful that at least one of the models fits the data well, we now have three models and we need to determine which model fits the data the best. For this we can perform a nested likelihood ratio test to compare models. We start by going from the most complex to the least complex model, so we will compare models 6 and 8. The p-value returned from performing the nested likelihood ratio test on models 6 and 8 is 0.006745816, which tells us that we prefer model 8 and eliminate model 6. We then do the same test with models 8 and 5 and return a p-value of 0.03414934. This means that we prefer model 5 and eliminate model 8.

Thus through the use of chi-squared tests based on \(G^2\) and nested likelihood ratio tests we have determined that model 5 fits the data the best and states that fatigue is independent of intervention group given weakness.

Problem 4

Summarize your findings in the statistical analyses you perform in the first three problems. Is weakness related to fatigue? If so, in which way? Is the intervention effective in altering the levels of weakness or fatigue? Are the findings from your regression models consistent with those from your loglinear models?

These findings make quite a bit of sense. What we found in part 1 is that we can accurately predict fatigue based on weakness and the intervention group. What we found in part 2 is that we can accurately predict weakness based on fatigue and intervention group. What these two parts showed is that there is clearly a non-independent relationship between fatigue and weakness when holding the intervention group constant.

This is consistent with our findings from our log-linear models. What we found in problem 3 was that both models five and six explain one of the symptoms using the intervention group and given the other symptom. This is similar with what we found in problems 1 and 2 since they both showed that one of the symptoms give us information about the other.

To understand the effect of the intervention group we can return to the models from problems 1 and 2 to see the coefficients. Based on our chosen model from problem 1 we know that when holding all else constant, being a part of the intervention group decreased the log-odds of fatigue being reported as a 1 (by .29) and reported as a 2 (by .36). However, we see that being in the intervention group, when holding all else constant, increased the log-odds of reporting a fatigue of 3 minimally (by 0.096). This means that the intervention may have assisted in decreasing mild fatigue (reports of a 1 or 2), it was not effective in decreasing the most intense fatigue (reporting a 1). All of this can be seen in Figure 1 below.

Figure 1

Based on our chosen model from problem 2, we can see that while holding all else constant, being a part of the intervention group decreases the log-odds likelihood of reporting a 1, 2, and 3 level weakness by 0.22, 0.289, and 0.76 respectively. What this tells us, since this model was deemed to be a good fit of the data is that we have statistically significant evidence to suggest that the intervention deceased weakness in patients. #libraries 
library(nnet)
library(lmtest)
library(AICcmodavg)
library(tidyverse)
library(gtExtras)
#load in the data
data = read.csv("joachim-ic.csv") 
#create a three way table
mytable <- xtabs(~ ssc2 + ssc4 + ic, data = data) 
#check that the table works for IC 0 and IC 1 
mytable

## 
##     ssc4
## ssc2   0   1   2   3

#SSC4 = Fatigue
#SSC2 = Weakness
#making the data work for regression models
X = as.factor(data[,"ssc2"]) # weakness
Y = as.factor(data[,"ssc4"]) # fatigue 
time = as.factor(data[,"time"]) #dont care
ic = data[,"ic"] #intervention

#fitting all the models
M1 = multinom(Y ~ 1)
## # weights:  8 (3 variable)

## final  value 1792.412866 
## converged
AIC(M1)
## [1] 3590.826
BIC(M1)
## [1] 3606.434
M2 = multinom(Y ~ X)
## # weights:  20 (12 variable)
## initial  value 1861.793327 
## iter  10 value 1414.533298
## iter  20 value 1388.443272
## iter  20 value 1388.443272
## iter  20 value 1388.443272
## final  value 1388.443272 
## converged
AIC(M2)

BIC(M2)

M3 = multinom(Y ~ ic)

## initial  value 1861.793327 
## iter  10 value 1784.371085
## final  value 1784.370960 
## converged
AIC(M3)
## [1] 3580.742
BIC(M3)

M4 = multinom(Y ~ X + ic)

# create df
model <- NA
model_name <- NA
aic <- NA
bic <- NA

table1 <- data.frame(model, model_name, aic, bic)

table1[1, ] <- list("1)", "Fatigue ~ 1", "3590.826", "3606.434")
table1[nrow(table1) + 1, ] <- list("2)", "Fatigue ~ Weakness", "2800.887", "2863.318")
table1[nrow(table1) + 1, ] <- list("3)", "Fatigue ~ Intervention Group", "3580.742", "3611.958")
table1[nrow(table1) + 1, ] <- list("4)", "Fatigue ~ Weakness + Intervention Group", "2798.225", "2876.265")
table1[nrow(table1) + 1, ] <- list("5)", "Fatigue ~ Weakness * Intervention Group", "2806.126", "2930.990")

table1_pretty <- table1 %>% 
  gt() %>% 
  tab_header(title = "Fatigue Regression Models") %>% 
  cols_label(model = "Model", model_name = "", aic = "AIC", bic = "BIC") %>% 
  gt_add_divider(columns = "model_name") %>% 
  gt_add_divider(columns = "aic") %>% 
  cols_align(align = c("left"), columns = c(aic, bic)) %>% 
  gt_highlight_rows(
    columns = everything(),
    rows = c(4), 
    font_weight = "normal")  %>%
  tab_footnote(footnote = "Table 1: The five regression models fit for the fatigue variable. The model with the smallest AIC and BIC is highlighted.")
